A young participant adds to River of Recovery, a 24-foot community mural created as part of Williams Lake First Nation's National Addictions Awareness Week programming. A painted salmon is one of the images community members added to the Chilcotin River scene in River of Recovery. A young participant holds up paint-covered hands while working on the River of Recovery mural. Spider-man appears among the figures community members painted along the riverbank in River of Recovery. Artist Tiffany Jorgensen and George Warr stand beside River of Recovery, a community mural art created as part of Williams Lake First Nation's National Awareness Week programming. A 24-foot mural painted during Williams Lake First Nation’s National Addictions Awareness Week will hang at the Nation’s Cwelcwélt Health Station. Titled River of Recovery, the mural depicts the Chilcotin River at Farwell Canyon, where dozens of community members added images and symbols of healing and recovery and tributes to loved ones they’ve lost at Elizabeth Grouse Gymnasium on the closing day on Nov. 6. The youngest contributor to the River of Recovery mural was about five and a half months old. Her mother added a tiny footprint. Several elders in their 80s also contributed. The Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) l Addiction Awareness Week programming took place from Nov. 2 to Nov. 6. The opening day began with a community march and candlelight vigil, and the final day’s event included naloxone training. The local week programming took place ahead of National Addictions Awareness Week, which runs from Nov. 15 to Nov. 21 across Canada. Over the five days, WLFN hosted workshops, community gatherings, wellness services, and recovery activities. 1f8430898597dae8f01640ef53bf1b58.text: Chad Marchand was among the vendors at last Saturday's Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market with his custom hardwood cutting boards. It was everything locally made at the Williams Lake Tourism Discovery Centre on Saturday, Nov. 14 where the annual Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market was held. More than 700 people filtered in to explore 28 vendors set up on all three floors offering a variety of wares. New this year was Chad Marchand of Williams Lake with his custom hardwood cutting boards. The professional forester with BC Timber Sales handcrafts the end grain boards in a small shop in his family’s backyard where they are also sealed with beeswax. “I wanted one for my own brisket making,” Marchand said with a laugh, adding he still doesn’t have one for himself just yet. “Every time one comes out I can’t decide this is the one for me so I just keep on making them.” It has been approximately five to six months that Marchand has started making his unique cutting boards that he typically does after work along his other hobby, gardening. Tourism Discovery Centre operations manager and Williams Lake and District Chamber of Commerce executive assistant Tanya Hutchison called Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market a great way to bring local vendors and showcase their artisan skills with the community. Their products also might not be necessarily found in any other store. Marchand hopes to participate in other upcoming local holiday markets and has already signed up to be part of next year’s Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market.

Tŝilhqot’in ʔEten Nadiltil, TEN, a majority Indigenous owned construction company, has partnered with Kamloops based Dawson Civil to expand its civil construction and infrastructure operations across B.C. Dandzen Development LP, the economic development arm of the Tŝilhqot’in National Government, founded TEN in 2017 and hold a 51 per cent stake in the company. In a media release, TEN board director Dalton Baptiste said the company was founded to make roads safer in Tŝilhqot’in territory and help diversify the local economy amid a downturn in forestry. He said TEN now aims to work with Indigenous communities and businesses across B.C. on large infrastructure projects that create jobs and business opportunities for Tŝilhqot’inpeople. This new partnership bring together Indigenous leadership and over a century of experience in complex infrastructure, mining, and industrial environments. Tŝilhqot’in National Government represents the six Tŝilhqot’in in communities: Tl’etinqox, ʔEsdilagh, Yuneŝit’in, Tŝideldel, Tl’esqox, and Xeni Gwet’in. Baptiste added in the media release “That vision has not changed, it has only expanded. We are growing a company that will continue to create lasting employment and business opportunities for our people and redefine what Indigenous-led enterprise looks like in British Columbia.” He added, “Our goal is to partner with Indigenous communities and companies across the province to deliver large-scale infrastructure projects that benefit all British Columbians with respect for the land and Tŝilhqot’in values always guiding our work.” TEN’s work includes earthworks, regional and municipal infrastructure, and mining construction. The company also serves the forestry, mining, energy, civil and municipal, industrial, and road maintenance sectors. ccee08dc4d9b2794e28f9893f2ef6cc7.text: Students can browse graduation outfits at Ever After Attire's Borrowed Magic pop-up in Williams Lake on Nov. 21 and borrow an outfit for free. Williams Lake students looking for something to wear to graduation can try on dresses and suits and take an outfit home for free at Ever After Attire’s Borrowed Magic pop-up. The drop-in event runs from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21, in the Graham Kelsey Room at the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Centre. Admission is free and no registration is required. Nikki Blodgett, program coordinator for Ever After Attire remembers looking for a graduation dress when she was in high school. “Shopping for a grad dress was so expensive and I wondered how everyone could do it,” Blodgett said. She took over the program from Williams Lake photographer Rick Magnell and has been running it for about a year. Ever After Attire’s lending program is open to graduates in the Williams Lake area regardless of financial circumstances. Blodgett said the collection includes about 125 dresses, along with suits, dress pants, shirts, ties, dress shoes and heels. A change room will be available, and students can bring a friend or parent to help with fittings. Volunteers can also help students choose an outfit or lace up a dress. Ever After Attire said seamstress Dominique Bouchard will be on hand to help with small fixes, such as loose straps or fasteners, and offer advice on alterations. Students who find an outfit they want to borrow can leave their name and phone number and take it home that day. Dresses and suits are due back to Cariboo Corner within two weeks after graduation. Wanda Ranson from Dream Day Bouquet Floral Design will be offering a free floral-themed craft, and Sparkle Booth will provide free photos. Permanent jewellery will also be available for a fee by appointment, Blodgett said. Mary Forbes shows fabrics to repurpose into poppies and shares wartime stories during an up cycled poppy workshop in Williams Lake on Nov. 8, ahead of Remembrance Day. Now in its third year, the DIY poppy workshop in Williams Lake brings people together to turn reclaimed fabrics into poppies, share family stories and honour those who served ahead of Remembrance Day. Materials from the Salvation Army thrift store find new life as handmade poppies during the third annual up cycled poppy workshop at NEXT GENeral in Williams Lake. Mary Forbes displays poppies she made in previous years at the third annual DIY poppy workshop on Sunday, Nov. 8 at NEXT GENeral in Williams Lake The DIY poppy workshop in Williams Lake was more than creating flowers from upcycled materials. It was a chance to share stories of wartime and honour those who served and sacrificed, including families and children. The workshop took place on Sunday, Nov. 8 from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. at NEXT GENeral – Mercantile + Refillery (NGMR). It was hosted by store owner Dani Gastaldello and Mary Forbes, both representing the Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society (CCCS) Waste Wise program. Waste Wise is an environmental education and community outreach program managed by the CCCS, with funding in part from the City of Williams Lake and the Cariboo Regional District, with a mission to teach residents to rethink their waste and reduce the amount going to local landfills. The free drop-in workshop invited residents to turn reclaimed fabrics, old jewellery and buttons into unique poppy pins. The recycled material was donated by the Salvation Army thrift store. Now, in it’s third year, the workshop has grown from a discovery Forbes made while helping clean out the Potato House attic. d3f8ec8166909cda31f3692d79e0e82a.text: Anti-SOGI Protesters and pro-SOGI counter-protesters took to the streets in Vancouver on Wednesday, Sept. 20, 2023. During the provincial election campaign’s home stretch in late October, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson held a boisterous rally in a Surrey warehouse, hitting his major talking points to thunderous approval. One of the biggest applause lines came when he mentioned the B.C. schools initiative called Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123. “We are going to get our grades up, and we are going to repeal SOGI!” Doerkson shouted. SOGI 123 is a set of resources provided by an organization called the ARC Foundation to help teachers talk about sexual orientation and gender with students, with the goal being to reduce stigma and bullying. It is sometimes mistakenly referred to as a curriculum and confused with sex education, which it is not. Christy Clark’s B.C. Liberal government created it via a ministerial directive in 2016, and over the past 10 years SOGI-inclusive learning has been threaded into the education system. (Clark sat ringside at Doerkson’s Surrey rally, cheering him on.) As a set of educational resources rather than a law, SOGI 123 is not technically subject to repeal. So what could Doerkson mean in practice when he says he wants to repeal SOGI? And how will schools continue to work to protect gender-diverse students from bullying and harassment? This past summer, the B.C. government ended its partnership with ARC, leading the foundation to wind down operations. In some sense, this means that the province’s schools have already moved beyond SOGI 123. In a news release, then-Conservative Party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and the party’s education critic at the time, Lynne Block, hailed the termination of the ARC partnership as the “end of SOGI.” According to B.C. c99cecf48a644b68453a76c90064410a.text: Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital | Williams Lake Tribune Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to raise $3.5 million to bring a da Vinci Surgical System to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital. Various images of the da Vinci Surgical System Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to bring to the hospital in Nanaimo. A non-profit intends to bring the first surgical robotic system to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital for more precise surgeries. In a press release, Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation says it hopes to raise $3.5 million in its 2026/27 winter fundraising drive for the da Vinci Surgical System for use at NRGH – it would be the first robotics program in Nanaimo and the second on Vancouver Island. A “robotic-assisted surgical platform,” the system utilizes a doctor’s hand motions, translating them “into precise, real-time movements of miniaturized instruments inside the body,” according to the press release. “It combines high-definition 3-D visualization, instruments with greater range of motion than the human hand, and advanced features to support highly precise, minimally invasive surgery,” it noted. Robotic-assisted surgery has become the norm for care in hospitals across the continent and affords hospital personnel the ability to “operate with enhanced precision, visualization and control through smaller incisions, including in areas of the body that can be difficult to reach using conventional surgical instruments.” At first, the da Vinci Surgical System will be utilized for procedures such as those for kidneys, colorectal and prostates, with intention to add ear-nose-throat surgery and gynecology, in the future. Residents in the North Thompson Valley are raising the alarm about service issues with Telus after a week-long cell-service outage impacted communities along Highway 5. According to Telus’ service status map, a “degradation of wireless services in Clearwater” began on Nov. 7 and lasted until Nov. 13. Impacted services included mobile data, mobile text and mobile voice, according to the outage report. While the map showed Clearwater as the primary location of the degradation, it was members of communities beyond Clearwater along Highway 5 who experienced the worst service cutoffs. The issue became so pressing for some people that one posted to the Vavenby BC Info Board, a private local Facebook group, the morning of Nov. 13, trying to push for immediate action and advocacy to Telus to address the problem. The *Clearwater Times* attempted to contact this individual, but has been unable to reach them. The post included a letter template, addressed to Kamloops-Thompson-Nicola MP Frank Caputo, urging the parliamentarian to advocate on behalf of the community about rural cell service reliability in the riding. The post also suggested sending the letter to Thompson-Nicola Regional District (TNRD) Area A director Usoff Tsao. I am writing as a constituent in [Your Community] regarding the ongoing Telus cell outage along Highway 5. While service is working inside Clearwater and Barriere, rural residents between Vavenby and the Sun Peaks highway corridor remain without cell service as of today, leaving thousands of residents—including vulnerable seniors—without emergency communication. The *Clearwater Times* has been in touch with the office of MP Caputo about the issue and will update this story if any comments are received. 74557973ceca5843bd1a59c5810d486b.text: A B.C. Supreme Court judge dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought forward by the former mayor of Quesnel’s wife against a city councillor over comments made during a 2024 council meeting. In a decision published on Nov. 10, Justice Tindale ruled that Quesnel Coun. Laurey-Anne Roodenburg’s statements about Pat Morton’s distribution of a book questioning the findings surrounding residential schools were protected under the Protection of Public Participation Act. Morton, the wife of former Quesnel Mayor Ron Paull, filed the lawsuit following comments Roodenburg made during a March 19, 2024, council meeting. According to the court document, the controversy began after Morton distributed copies of _Grave Error: How the Media Misled Us (and the Truth about Residential Schools),_ which she had purchased in February 2024. On March 19, 2024, Lhtako Dene Nation sent a letter to the mayor and council expressing concern about the book, saying it questioned the existence of residential schools and whether cultural genocide had occurred. The letter called on council to reaffirm its Memorandum of Understanding with the Nation and offered to have Elders who attended residential schools share first-hand knowledge of their experiences with council. According to the court document, during the meeting in March, Paull identified his wife as the person distributing the book and said he had not read it. Roodenburg, who was serving as the city’s Indigenous Liaison at the time, criticized Morton’s actions, saying they showed a lack of respect for the mayor’s position and were causing harm to members of First Nations communities. “I respect the fact that people have the right to their own opinions, but what I don’t see here is the respect that your wife has shown you in your role as mayor of this community,” Roodenburg said at the time, according to the court document. “We know that what has happened reflects not only on you, but on council and on our community as a whole. ff61a761ba6649050660d9c61bb3073a.text: B.C. NDP calls for opposition to Quebecor’s Telus takeover bid | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. NDP calls for opposition to Quebecor’s Telus takeover bid The Telus Park building on 64 Avenue in Surrey, pictured on Nov. 18, 2026. Interim B.C. NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside is calling on the incoming government to oppose Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, warning it would reduce competition and could lead to higher prices for British Columbians. “Consolidating two major national telecommunications players will inevitably reduce competition in our market, leading to fewer choices, diminished service quality, and higher monthly bills for families and small businesses,” Whiteside said in a letter addressed to incoming premier Lorne Doerkson. Telus is B.C. based, while Quebecor is headquartered in Montreal. Both companies compete in B.C.’s budget cell-phone market: Telus owns Public Mobile, and Quebecor owns Freedom Mobile. In addition to reducing competition, Whiteside says the shift to East Coast ownership would be bad for B.C.’s economy. Telus is headquartered in Vancouver and has multiple new office buildings under construction. “For decades, Telus has been a cornerstone of British Columbia’s technology and telecommunications sector,” she said. “The prospect of an out-of-province acquisition raises serious concerns for working families, businesses, and our provincial economy.” The takeover bid, which offers cash and shares, would still need regulatory approval. Quebecor argues it would create a “strong pan-Canadian competitor” to compete with other national providers and foreign competitors. Doerkson responded to Whiteside’s letter by saying he wants to ensure British Columbians have choice, competitive prices and reliable cell service. He also wants local jobs preserved. “There are legitimate questions raised by a change in ownership and must be fully considered as part of any approval process,” he said in a written statement.
